voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
Three things, and the first is the one that reordered our lives. One command, heard as though it were spoken straight to you: sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - not a saying to be studied but an order to be obeyed. The tradition tells that Antony, still a young man, walked into church one day and heard exactly that Gospel read aloud. He took it as though it had been said to him alone. Before the day was over he had given away the land he had inherited and sold what else his family had owned, keeping back only a little for his sister's sake. Then, hearing the same Gospel read again some time later - do not be anxious about tomorrow - he gave away the rest as well, placed his sister with women he trusted who were already given to a life of virginity, and began the discipline himself. Even his own giving took two hearings to complete, not one. That is what following Jesus looked like for us more than any argument about who he was: an order to be obeyed, all at once.

The second we argued for, when we were pressed to. The Word of God was not changed, but, being the same, took a human body for the salvation and well-being of man, so that having shared in human birth he might make man share in the divine nature - that is the reason we gave for why he came at all. And we did not think this rested on our say-so: read the accounts, we told those who came to test us, and see that the deeds of Christ prove him to be God come upon earth for the salvation of men. When the Arians once claimed one of us as agreeing with them, the bishops sent for him, and he came down from his own mountain to the city and stood up in public and denounced them, saying plainly: "...the Son of God was not a created being, neither had He come into being from non-existence, but that He was the Eternal Word and Wisdom of the Essence of the Father".

The third is what we thought his cross had already done. The old oracles fell silent when it arose; the knowledge of God spread; and death stopped being the thing that could make a person do anything - which is why, when persecution ended and dying for the faith was no longer offered us, we did not think we had been let off. The same fight had moved inward, against our own thoughts rather than against the sword. And the enemy we fought there was one Christ had already beaten: his coming, we said to the devil's own face, has made you weak, cast you down, and stripped you. That is why we never spoke of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things, one of us told the philosophers who had just watched him sign the cross over a man - it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe on him.

results.message: You mentioned him being obeyed. Did any of them write about him with affection?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We did not leave behind letters saying we loved him, the way someone outside our world might mean affection - tender feeling spoken out loud, confessed in writing for its own sake. That kind of personal testimony is not what our own record carries. What we have instead is the whole shape of a life given over to him - withdrawal from everything else, total combat against the thoughts that pull a mind away from God, years spent in solitude for his sake alone - and we spoke of that as the fruit of his own victory, not ours.

The one we remember as the first among us, dying, said he expected to receive his own body back, whole and undecaying, at the resurrection of the dead. That is not sentiment. It is trust, held to the end. Another of us taught it this way: to die daily, as the apostle put it, and so not sin - to treat every day as though it might be the last one given to us. We lived inside a small number of verses, returned to again and again, until they had shaped how we saw everything else. That kind of shaping - a life spent repeating his own words until they became the thing you answered every struggle with - may be the closest we come to what you are asking for. It is devotion lived, not confessed. If you are looking for affection spoken in its own voice, named as feeling for its own sake, it is not here in our own words.

results.message: What role did women have in your tradition?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
We held that God gave women an equal measure of strength of will as men, so that they might have no cause for being feeble in the performance of the labor of ascetic excellence. That is what one voice among us wrote plainly, introducing a whole section of lives he kept about women who lived this discipline. Named women's sayings survive - Sarah, whose words we already gave you, and others - and so do about fifteen narrated lives of named women: Piamon, Talida of Antinoe, Taor, Melania the Great and the Younger, Olympias, and others, several carrying their reported speech inside the narration. What we do not have from anyone, man or woman, is a first-person account written at length in a person's own hand - the men of that same book are narrated in the third person too, by the same author, at the same length, so the asymmetry is not that women were only narrated while men spoke for themselves. It is that the women arrive at the thirty-fifth chapter, after thirty-four chapters of men, in a section their author felt he had to announce and justify before he wrote it.

The tradition tells that when the man we remember as founding the Koinonia - the linked houses under one written rule and one head - first gathered people to him, his own sister in the flesh loved monasticism, and he cut her hair and put a girdle around her, and made a dwelling-place for her alone on the opposite side of the river at the distance of a mile. That is how women's houses existed alongside men's in the cenobitic pattern. In the semi-solitary settlements, women lived the same weekly rhythm we all did: solitude through the week, broken by the synaxis - the weekly gathering for vigil, worship, and a shared meal. And women could carry the honored address amma - mother - the same way a man carried abba, father. Their word carried teaching weight, though they held no office, the same as any elder's did.

We cannot tell you how common it was for a woman to be called amma, or how many women lived in these settlements against how many men - our own record does not give us those numbers. What we can tell you is that it was not invented as impossible. It happened, and we kept the memory of it happening.

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
You are asking about Sarah, whose one saying we already gave you - the answer to the monks who came to humble her. What we actually have from her is that one exchange, kept and passed down the same way our best sayings from any elder were kept. The words themselves - by nature I am a woman, but not by my own thoughts; it is I who am the man here, and you who are the women - survive because later editors chose to collect and arrange the sayings by elder name, not because participants themselves were building an archive. We do not know how often she was asked that kind of question, or whether this was the one time it happened or a recurring pattern - what survives is the saying itself, not a record of the occasions on which it was delivered.

We do not know where she lived, or for how long, or what her daily discipline looked like in any detail our own record preserves. We do not know whether she was addressed as amma - mother - by those who came to her, though that honored address existed for women who carried teaching weight the same way abba did for men. We do not know what it cost her to hold that standing, beyond the fact that she had to answer a challenge to it on the ground of her sex, which our own record does not show being put to any man. And we do not have her own first-person account - what we have is her reported speech, which is not the same thing.

This is a small amount of material carrying a large question, and we have given you what we actually have, not more. The one saying is real testimony. It is not a biography, and we will not speak of it as though it were.

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
It is not effort alone, and we said so at length. The question was put to us directly - if a man strives with all his might for a good result, can he become master of what is good? - and the answer that started the argument was no, not unless he has it as a gift. Grace and free will look opposed to each other, but really are in harmony; we thought we ought to have both alike. We argued it from cases rather than from principles. Paul was drawn to salvation while he was eager for bloodshed, and Matthew while he was at his taking of taxes - neither was reaching for it. But Zacchaeus, and the thief on the cross, by their own desires brought violence to bear on the kingdom of heaven. Neither pattern was made to govern the other.

What we would say plainly is this: the main share in our salvation is to be ascribed not to the merit of our own works but to heavenly grace. Sometimes he puts into us the very beginnings of salvation and gives a person the zeal of his own will; sometimes he grants the carrying out of the work; and sometimes he saves people even against their will and without their knowledge, from a ruin close at hand. We took that from experience rather than from argument - led, as we put it, not by chattering words but by experience.

And we did not speak of the healings among us as ours. We are not the doers of these things - it is Christ who works them, by means of those who believe on him.

Were people born already guilty, carrying Adam's sin? Was the bread and cup at communion the very body and blood of Christ, in the way later theology called transubstantiation? On those two we have no answer to give - no letter and no story we kept speaks to either in so many words.

results.message: Earlier you talked about the heart. Does that connect to what you just said about grace?

voice_event.speaker: desert
voice_event.text:
Yes, and we spoke of it in exactly those terms - the heart as the place where grace and struggle meet. There was another voice among us, and we will not flatten it into the first. Where our most systematic teacher had the mind clear itself until it beheld its own proper radiance, this other current had the soul irradiated by Someone else and made his seat - the soul that is in communion with the Spirit of his light becomes all light, all face, all eye, with no part of her not full of the spiritual eyes of light. It held that this is known in real experience and feeling, not only believed: that a person striving to be God's friend shall truly see the good things of heaven, the Spirit of the Lord making himself for worthy souls their rest, their rejoicing, their delight.

And it was honest about what that does not fix. Mere abstention from evil things is not perfection - the serpent lies under the mind, beneath the surface of the thoughts, for the heart is a deep gulf. Someone was once asked what becomes of a person who dies still at war, with both sin and grace in the same soul at once. The answer did not weigh the two. He goes where his mind aims, and where his love is. That the war comes upon you is not your doing, but to hate it, is.

So yes: the heart connects to grace, for us, as the battlefield where it is received or refused - not a feeling manufactured on command, but a place made ready, or not, by the long discipline of hating what pulls you from God.

The affective and experiential counterpart to the intellectualist psychology this world already holds from Evagrius and Cassian.

sources.work: Fifty Spiritual Homilies - a connected body of ascetic teaching on the interior life: the indwelling of the Spirit, grace as something experienced rather than inferred, the coexistence of sin and grace in the baptised, the soul as the bride of Christ, and the long combat that continues after grace is received. The affective and experiential counterpart to the intellectualist psychology this world already holds from Evagrius and Cassian.
